analysis.one_liner: Bans for-profit corporations from operating political action committees, allowing them only for nonprofits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote, dying in committee with 5 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal campaign finance law so that only nonprofit corporations could sponsor a corporate political action committee — the kind of PAC that pools voluntary donations from a company's executives and employees. For-profit companies with existing PACs would have to shut them down and give away their remaining money within a year. The bill was referred to the House committee that oversees election law and never went any further.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and candidates who rely on small individual donations, by removing one structured channel through which for-profit corporations fund federal campaigns and build relationships with lawmakers. Nonprofit corporations would keep PAC rights that for-profit companies lose.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Federal Election Campaign Act so only corporations that are tax-exempt nonprofits under section 501(c) may establish or operate a separate segregated fund for political purposes, removing for-profit corporations from that authority [S3].
Requires any existing for-profit corporate PAC to terminate and disburse its entire balance within one year of enactment [S2][S3].
Restricts who corporate PACs may solicit from, removing stockholders and their families from the pool of allowable contributors [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit corporations that currently operate political action committees lose a regulated channel for political giving, and the members of Congress and party committees that receive corporate PAC money lose that funding source.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations with PACs and their beneficiaries

drawbacks.text: The ban covers only PACs sponsored by for-profit corporations; labor unions and nonprofits keep their PACs, and money can move to super PACs and other outside-spending vehicles that the bill does not touch, so total corporate influence over elections could shift to less transparent channels rather than shrink [S2][S3].

A good-faith objection is that corporate PACs are funded by voluntary employee contributions and are publicly disclosed, so banning them may reduce transparency and fundraising support for candidates without limiting overall corporate political spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses one specific, disclosed fundraising channel for corporate money but leaves super PACs, dark-money groups, and union PACs untouched, so its practical effect on who influences elections is uncertain. It would remove a visible, regulated mechanism, which is a real but modest gain for voters, and it dies without ever having been weighed on its merits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House committee that handles election law the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Max Rose of New York introduced the Ban Corporate PACs Act in the House on November 15, 2019, with Josh Harder of California, Joe Kennedy, and Antonio Delgado joining the introduction [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the Committee on House Administration, the committee with jurisdiction over campaign finance law, that same day [S5].
The bill never received a markup, a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; the only action in its entire history is the referral [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 5 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 231 House Democrats, and no Republicans [S4].
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021, and the bill died with the Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that operate political action committees keep that funding channel, and the incumbent lawmakers who receive corporate PAC money are unaffected. Voters are left with campaign finance rules unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations with PACs and incumbent lawmakers

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so there is no roll call; all 5 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill, while most House Democrats declined to sign on and the Democratic-run committee never acted.

industries.industry: For-profit corporations with political action committees
industries.note: The bill eliminates their separate segregated funds — a regulated, disclosed channel for corporate-backed campaign spending — within one year. Companies would keep other channels, including super PACs, but this one closes.
Only nonprofits would retain the right to sponsor corporate PACs, leaving them a fundraising channel their for-profit peers lose. The bill imposes nothing on them.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and party committees that receive corporate PAC contributions
industries.note: Corporate PAC money is a major fundraising source for many incumbents; the bill would cut it off for candidates who take it, which helps explain the absence of support among lawmakers.
